chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Sahl, from Zakariyya ibn Adam, who said:

I asked Al-Reza (peace be upon him) about a people from the enemies who reconciled (signed a peace treaty), then they breached it, and perhaps they breached it because justice had not been done upon them. Is it correct to buy from their captives? So he (peace be upon him) said: 'If it was from the enemies who had manifested their enmity, so buy from them (their captives), and if it was a number who were alienated and had been unjust, so do not buy from their captives'.

He (the narrator) said: 'And I asked him (peace be upon him) about a captive of Al-Daylam who had stolen from each other and the Muslims had attacked them without an Imam (peace be upon him), is buying them Permissible? He (peace be upon him) said: 'When they had been endorsed with the slavery so there is no problem with buying them'.

He (the narrator) said: 'And I asked him (peace be upon him) about a people from the ones under the responsibility (Ahl Al-Zimma) who have been hit by hunger (famine), so a man comes over with his son, so he says, 'This is for you, so feed him, and he would be a slave for you'. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'You cannot sell the free, for it is not correct for you, nor from the people under the responsibility (Ahl Al-Zimma)'.

key_terms.أَهْلِ الذِّمَّةِ: People of the covenant/tribute (non-Muslims living under Muslim rule)
key_terms.صَالَحُوا: They reconciled or signed a peace treaty

ai.seo_question: What are the conditions for buying captives from enemies who broke peace treaties or from specific groups like the Daylam and Ahl Al-Zimma?
ai.summary: Imam al-Rida (AS) provides nuanced criteria for the validity of enslaving captives, distinguishing between those with manifest enmity and those who merely breached treaties, while also addressing the specific context of the Daylamis. The narration further clarifies the principle of 'free status preservation' by ruling that giving food to a free person during famine does not automatically confer slave status, a key distinction in Shia jurisprudence. This highlights the importance of intent and social status in determining the permissibility of purchasing slaves from different communities.
